Finance is not a reporting function. You find that out the week somebody with
money asks a question your file cannot answer.

Then a term sheet arrives and the mirror is asked to argue. A diligence
question is not a request for a number. It is a request for the reasoning that
produced the number, and the reasoning either exists in writing or it gets
improvised, in a data room, by a founder who has been awake since five.

There is a seed round I talk about because the founder has told the story
himself on a podcast, so it is his to give away and not mine. The round stalled
for five weeks. Not on valuation, not on the market, not on a single number in
the model. It stalled on a revenue recognition policy nobody had ever written
down. Everyone knew how the company recognised revenue. Nobody could hand over
a paragraph saying so, and until that paragraph existed the investor could not
close.

Five weeks of a founder's life, and a lawyer's bill, for a paragraph.

So the test I would apply to your own file is not whether the numbers tie out.
It is whether the three decisions you argue about most in your company exist as
paragraphs anywhere. Not slides. Paragraphs, with a date on them, that somebody
who does not like you could read.

If they do not, your finance function is a mirror, and the first person who
negotiates with you will find that out before you do.

Nadia Feriel, fractional CFO for seed and Series A B2B SaaS.
I build the model and I sit in the room when it gets argued about.
